description: A low mangrove shrub of tidal-stream margins and the inland edge of brackish forests, usually less spiny than Acanthus ilicifolius.
physical_characteristics: White to pale flowers in terminal spikes
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, narrow elliptic to lanceolate leaves with mostly entire or only slightly toothed margins and a pointed tip.
root_characteristics: A spreading woody rootstock anchors soft bank soil; it has no specialized stilt roots or pneumatophores.
ecological_importance: Provides low vegetation cover and refuge
Adds flowering and seed resources to mangrove-edge food webs
history: Martin Vahl published the species in 1791. Philippine botanical records place it along tidal streams and inland mangrove borders.
scientific_study: Useful for studies of mangrove associates, understory diversity, salt exposure, and comparison with the more strongly spined Acanthus ilicifolius.
conservation_information: Protect upper mangrove margins from clearing
Verify flowers and leaf margins because Acanthus species are easily confused
interesting_facts: Its name refers to the early loss or absence of conspicuous bracts
The capsule can eject seeds when mature
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Protect native upper-mangrove vegetation and verify the species using several plant parts.

description: A robust mangrove-edge shrub recognized by glossy holly-like leaves and showy blue-violet flowers.
physical_characteristics: Large pale blue to violet flowers
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, thick, glossy leaves with strongly toothed or spiny margins, although some shoots may be nearly entire.
root_characteristics: A creeping woody rootstock and branching underground roots bind muddy banks; aerial roots are absent.
ecological_importance: Provides nectar and cover at mangrove margins
history: Carl Linnaeus published the species in 1753. The Philippine name Acanthus doloariu published by Blanco is treated as a synonym.
scientific_study: Frequently used in research on salt tolerance, mangrove associate zonation, pollination, and traditional plant use.
conservation_information: Avoid treating native stands as weeds during rehabilitation
Use several plant parts for identification
interesting_facts: The leaf resembles holly
Young or shaded leaves may have fewer spines
Its capsule uses a spring-like seed-dispersal mechanism
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Protect the landward mangrove buffer and verify variable leaf margins carefully.

description: A scrambling or climbing mangrove shrub with mostly spineless leaves and a restricted Southeast Asian distribution.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, narrow elliptic leaves with smooth, spineless margins and a pointed tip.
root_characteristics: Woody basal roots anchor climbing stems in brackish swamp soil; specialized aerial roots are absent.
ecological_importance: Improves representation of locally uncommon mangrove associates
history: Nathaniel Wallich published the name in 1831. Modern Philippine records confirm scattered native populations in brackish habitats.
scientific_study: Valuable for comparative Acanthus taxonomy and surveys of overlooked mangrove understory diversity.
conservation_information: Confirm climbing habit, white flowers, and smooth leaf margins
interesting_facts: It is the climbing Philippine mangrove Acanthus
Its leaves generally lack holly-like spines
Future CNN status: candidate only; verified public images are limited
conservation_note: Scattered populations make verified photographs and georeferenced records especially valuable.

description: A medium to tall pioneer mangrove of muddy seaward margins, deltas, and river mouths.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, narrow oblong to lanceolate leaves with a sharp tip, glossy upper surface, and pale underside.
root_characteristics: Numerous pencil-like pneumatophores rise from shallow horizontal cable roots.
history: Carl Ludwig Blume published the species in 1826. It is a standard field example of a pioneer mangrove.
scientific_study: Studied for pneumatophore function, salt regulation, sediment capture, and early mangrove succession.
conservation_information: Compare leaves and fruits with other Avicennia species
interesting_facts: Salt may be visible on leaf surfaces
Narrow pointed leaves distinguish it from Avicennia officinalis
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Protect pioneer mudflats and compare multiple traits before confirming an Avicennia species.

description: A broad-leaved Avicennia of inland riverbanks and relatively firm, lower-salinity mangrove mud.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, thick, broadly elliptic to obovate leaves are rounded at the tip and finely hairy beneath.
root_characteristics: Pencil pneumatophores arise from shallow cable roots; low supporting roots may occur.
ecological_importance: Supports estuarine fauna and organic matter cycling
history: Carl Linnaeus published the name in 1753. The epithet officinalis reflects historical association with prepared remedies.
scientific_study: Useful for research on salinity gradients, riverine zonation, leaf salt management, and Avicennia taxonomy.
conservation_information: Use leaf underside and flower traits for confirmation
interesting_facts: Leaves are broader than those of Avicennia alba
Fine hairs occur beneath leaves and on fruit
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Maintain inland estuarine hydrology and verify the hairy leaf underside and fruit.

description: A distinctive trunkless mangrove palm forming large stands along brackish tidal rivers.
leaf_characteristics: Very large pinnate fronds arise at ground level; the many leaflets are long, narrow, and lanceolate.
root_characteristics: Dense fibrous roots anchor an underground horizontal stem or rhizome.
ecological_importance: Provides habitat and sustainable community materials
history: Friedrich von Wurmb described Nypa fruticans in 1779. Nipa has long supported Philippine roofing, weaving, vinegar, and sugar production.
scientific_study: Studied for ancient palm biogeography, estuarine carbon storage, bank stabilization, and sustainable livelihoods.
conservation_information: Use sustainable frond and sap harvesting
interesting_facts: The visible plant has no upright trunk
Nypa fossils once occurred far beyond its modern range
Future CNN status: candidate only; palm-specific labels are needed
conservation_note: Protect tidal-river hydrology and harvest community products sustainably.

description: A small to medium upper-shore mangrove with white flowers and spoon-shaped leaves.
leaf_characteristics: Alternate, crowded, fleshy obovate leaves usually have a rounded or shallowly notched tip.
root_characteristics: Shallow spreading roots may form small peg-like pneumatophores in waterlogged soil.
ecological_importance: Links tidal forest with terrestrial coastal vegetation
history: Carl Ludwig Willdenow published the name in 1803. It is commonly paired with red-flowered Lumnitzera littorea in field keys.
scientific_study: Supports work on high-intertidal zonation, floral traits, drought tolerance, and mangrove-edge succession.
conservation_information: Use white flower color for identification
interesting_facts: Flowers are white, unlike Lumnitzera littorea
Leaves often look spoon-shaped
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Protect landward transition habitat and use flower color with leaf and fruit traits.

description: An upper-intertidal mangrove tree distinguished by vivid red flowers and rounded fleshy leaves.
leaf_characteristics: Alternate, crowded, thick obovate leaves have rounded, often shallowly notched tips.
root_characteristics: Shallow lateral roots may produce small pneumatophores where soil remains waterlogged.
history: The accepted combination was published in the nineteenth century. Its red flowers make it a prominent field-guide species.
scientific_study: Useful for research on pollination, phenology, high-shore tolerance, and differentiation from Lumnitzera racemosa.
interesting_facts: It is one of the few mangroves with bright red flowers
It occupies the drier mangrove edge
Future CNN status: candidate only; not currently recognized
conservation_note: Protect mature upper-shore trees and document their distinctive flowering season.

description: A slow-growing hard-wooded shrub or small tree of coral rock, limestone, and exposed high-tide shores.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, small, thick gray-green leaves are narrowly elliptic to oblong.
root_characteristics: Strong roots spread through rock crevices and surface substrate without conspicuous aerial roots.
ecological_importance: Provides habitat at the upper mangrove limit
history: Johann and Georg Forster published the species in 1776. Its dense wood has driven collection for construction and bonsai.
scientific_study: Important for studies of salt spray, rocky-shore zonation, slow growth, wood density, and collection pressure.
interesting_facts: Its wood is exceptionally dense
It grows where muddy-forest mangroves cannot
Future CNN data must exclude or tag shaped bonsai specimens
conservation_note: Philippine populations require protection from illegal collection despite a global Least Concern assessment.

description: A locally uncommon back-mangrove Sonneratia with broad leaves and flowers that usually lack petals.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite, thick, broad ovate to nearly circular leaves have a rounded tip.
root_characteristics: Short conical pneumatophores rise from cable roots in soft waterlogged mud.
history: Cornelis Backer published the species in 1920. Philippine records are scattered and make verified observations valuable.
scientific_study: Useful for rare-species monitoring and comparison with Sonneratia alba and Sonneratia caseolaris.
conservation_information: Confirm petal absence and broad leaves
interesting_facts: Flowers usually have no petals
Leaves can be almost circular
Future CNN status: candidate only; rarity limits balanced collection
conservation_note: Its Near Threatened status and scattered records make non-destructive monitoring important.

description: A rare soft-wooded mangrove native to the Philippines and Sulawesi, usually found along tidal creeks and mangrove margins.
leaf_characteristics: Obovate to elliptic-lanceolate leaves are crowded near twig ends and retain fine scales on both surfaces.
root_characteristics: Surface roots may form knobby pneumatophores around a gnarled trunk base.
history: Sebastian Vidal described its basionym in 1885, and Odoardo Beccari published the accepted combination in 1889.
scientific_study: Leaf scales, five-stamen flowers, cottony seed hairs, and its restricted range are important identification and conservation-study features.
conservation_information: Do not publish sensitive coordinates without expert review
interesting_facts: Its common name refers to cotton-like seed hairs
The accepted spelling is philippinensis
Future CNN status: candidate only; verified wild images are limited
conservation_note: This Endangered species requires non-destructive documentation and protection of every known population.

description: A large coastal and back-mangrove tree recognized by silvery leaf undersides and strongly keeled fruits.
leaf_characteristics: Alternate leathery leaves are green above and densely silver to coppery-scaled beneath.
root_characteristics: Mature trees develop strong plank buttresses; pneumatophores are generally absent.
ecological_importance: Links mangrove and coastal forest communities
history: The name was published in 1789. Older references placed the genus in Sterculiaceae, now included in Malvaceae.
scientific_study: Useful for studies of water-dispersed fruits, coastal canopy structure, and mangrove-to-beach-forest zonation.
conservation_information: Protect mature trees and buttress-root zones
interesting_facts: The silver leaf underside flashes like a mirror
Its keeled fruit can float
Future CNN status: candidate only; visual material is broadly available
conservation_note: Protect mature trees and the landward mangrove-to-coastal-forest transition.

description: A coastal Xylocarpus of exposed rocky or sandy shores, historically reported in Philippine guides as Xylocarpus moluccensis.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite compound leaves have two to four pairs of leathery ovate to heart-shaped leaflets with pointed tips.
root_characteristics: Conspicuous buttresses and pneumatophores are generally absent.
history: David Mabberley published the accepted combination in 1982. Older Philippine sources often applied the name Xylocarpus moluccensis.
scientific_study: Current Philippine flora treats older Philippine use of Xylocarpus moluccensis as a misapplied name for this species.
conservation_information: Keep the old name as a searchable alias
interesting_facts: Its seeds fit together like puzzle pieces
It usually lacks the large buttresses of Xylocarpus granatum
Future CNN status: candidate only; old-name confusion requires review
conservation_note: Record coastal substrate and use the Xylocarpus moluccensis alias only for historical matching.

description: An aromatic salt-tolerant shrub or small tree of exposed coral, rocky, and sandy shores.
leaf_characteristics: Small opposite brittle leaves contain visible oil glands and are aromatic when crushed.
root_characteristics: Cable-like surface roots may be exposed across rock or sand.
ecological_importance: Adds habitat where muddy-forest mangroves do not persist
history: Ferdinand von Mueller published the species in 1862. It is the only currently accepted species in its genus.
scientific_study: Useful for studies of exposed-shore zonation, salinity tolerance, aromatic oils, and substrate specialization.
interesting_facts: It is the sole species of Osbornia
Its crushed leaves are aromatic
Future CNN status: candidate only; verified image volume is moderate
conservation_note: Protect exposed rocky and coral-derived shore habitat and verify plants non-destructively.

description: A widespread small evergreen mangrove of sheltered tidal waterways, muddy estuaries, and creek banks.
leaf_characteristics: Alternate leathery obovate to elliptic leaves have rounded or shallowly notched tips and may show surface salt.
root_characteristics: Shallow spreading surface roots anchor firm mud; conspicuous specialized aerial roots are usually absent.
ecological_importance: Adds understory cover in sheltered mangroves
history: The species was first described under another genus in 1754; Francisco Manuel Blanco published the accepted combination in 1837.
scientific_study: Useful for research on cryptovivipary, salt management, sheltered-estuary zonation, and pollination.
conservation_information: Confirm curved fruit and clustered flowers
interesting_facts: Its curved fruit resembles a small horn
Salt may crystallize on its leaves
Future CNN status: candidate only; image availability is high
conservation_note: Protect tidal-creek vegetation and maintain natural freshwater and tidal connections.

description: A small Malesian mangrove of exposed rocky, coral, or sandy high-intertidal shores.
leaf_characteristics: Small leathery obovate leaves have rounded tips and may excrete salt.
root_characteristics: Shallow surface roots spread through rocky or sandy substrate.
history: The accepted name was published by Roemer and Schultes in 1819.
scientific_study: Useful for monitoring a relatively restricted Malesian mangrove and comparing substrate specialization within Aegiceras.
interesting_facts: Its mature curved fruits can be bright red
It favors more exposed shores than Aegiceras corniculatum
Future CNN status: candidate only; local images are limited
conservation_note: Document local populations and protect exposed rocky, coral-derived, and sandy habitat.

description: A medium true mangrove of sheltered estuaries and firm muddy or clay-rich substrates.
physical_characteristics: Smooth to finely fissured gray bark
leaf_characteristics: Opposite glossy elliptic leaves have pointed tips.
root_characteristics: Looping knee roots and short buttresses provide aeration and support.
history: Carl Linnaeus first described it under Rhizophora in 1753, and Carl Ludwig Blume published the accepted Bruguiera combination in 1827.
scientific_study: Useful for comparing knee roots, propagule form, and stand structure within Bruguiera.
conservation_information: Match restoration sites to firm substrate
Verify clustered flowers and slender propagules
interesting_facts: Its flowers are clustered rather than solitary
Looping knee roots emerge above mud
Future CNN status: candidate only; image availability is high
conservation_note: Protect sheltered estuarine stands and match any restoration planting to firm substrate.

description: A large upriver mangrove of lower-salinity waterways and interior forest that is flooded less often.
leaf_characteristics: Large opposite leathery elliptic leaves have acute tips.
root_characteristics: Knee roots, flanged buttresses, and occasional low stilt roots support mature trees.
ecological_importance: Adds structure to lower-salinity mangrove reaches
history: Joao de Loureiro described the basionym in 1790, and Jean Louis Marie Poiret published the accepted combination in 1816.
scientific_study: Useful for research on upriver zonation and comparison with Bruguiera gymnorrhiza and Bruguiera cylindrica.
conservation_information: Confirm the large flower and angular propagule
interesting_facts: The name sexangula refers to the propagule's six angles
It commonly grows farther upriver
Future CNN status: candidate only; image availability is high
conservation_note: Protect upriver stands and maintain both freshwater input and tidal flow.

description: A relatively uncommon Southeast Asian Ceriops now recognized as distinct from the South Asian Ceriops decandra.
leaf_characteristics: Opposite leathery leaves are oval to elliptical and often clustered near twig ends.
root_characteristics: Knee roots and a low buttressed base may develop in firm mud.
history: Carl Ludwig Blume described the species in the nineteenth century. Work published in 2009 supported its separation from Ceriops decandra.
scientific_study: It demonstrates how molecular and morphological evidence can correct long-used regional species names.
conservation_information: Compare it carefully with Ceriops tagal
interesting_facts: Older Philippine references may call it Ceriops decandra
Its compact inflorescence is diagnostic
Future CNN status: candidate only; public observations are sparse
conservation_note: Document local populations and require expert review before assigning old Ceriops decandra records.

description: A glossy-leaved shrub or small mangrove tree with fragrant pale flowers and distinctly grooved fruits.
physical_characteristics: Surface and occasional small stilt roots
leaf_characteristics: Opposite glossy leathery obovate to elliptic leaves have rounded tips.
root_characteristics: Surface roots and occasional small stilt roots may occur.
ecological_importance: Provides flowers and fruit for coastal fauna
history: Carl Friedrich Gaertner published the name in 1806. Historical Philippine names such as Ixora manilana are treated as synonyms.
scientific_study: Useful for Rubiaceae identification, high-intertidal zonation, pollination, and Philippine cultural-history lessons.
conservation_information: Treat the Manila name association as historical tradition
interesting_facts: The accepted spelling has one l in hydrophylacea
Its fruit has strong longitudinal grooves
Future CNN status: candidate only; fruit images are distinctive
conservation_note: Protect landward mangrove habitat and verify the species using its strongly grooved fruit.
